prompt: We call a $5$-tuple of integers *arrangeable* if its elements can be labeled $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $e$ in some order so that $a-b+c-d+e=29$. Determine all $2017$-tuples of integers $n_1, n_2, \dots, n_{2017}$ such that if we place them in a circle in clockwise order, then any $5$-tuple of numbers in consecutive positions on the circle is arrangeable.
answer: Only $n_1=n_2=\dots=n_{2017}=29$: after subtracting $29$, every five consecutive numbers have even sum, so all have the same parity (as $\gcd(5,2017)=1$), hence all are even, and infinite descent gives all zero.

solutions.title: Parity and infinite descent
solutions.body:
The tuple with all entries $29$ works, since $29-29+29-29+29=29$.

Conversely, put $m_i=n_i-29$ (indices mod $2017$). Because $(a-29)-(b-29)+(c-29)-(d-29)+(e-29)=a-b+c-d+e-29$, the condition becomes: any five consecutive $m$'s can be labelled so that $a-b+c-d+e=0$. Call such a circular tuple *balanced*. We show a balanced tuple is all zeros.

**Parity.** A signed sum $a-b+c-d+e$ has the same parity as $a+b+c+d+e$, so every window of five consecutive $m$'s has even sum. Subtracting the sums of the windows starting at $i$ and at $i+1$ gives $m_i\equiv m_{i+5}\pmod 2$. Since $\gcd(5,2017)=1$, stepping by $5$ visits every position, so all $m_i$ have the same parity; as the sum of five of them is even, they are all even.

**Descent.** If a balanced tuple consists of even numbers, halving every entry gives a balanced tuple again (the same labellings work). Suppose some $m_i\ne0$; let $2^e$ be the largest power of $2$ dividing all the $m_i$ (it exists because some entry is non-zero). Dividing by $2^e$ gives a balanced tuple with an odd entry, contradicting the parity step. Hence all $m_i=0$, i.e. all $n_i=29$. ∎

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB<AC$. Let $D$ be the intersection point of the internal bisector of angle $BAC$ and the circumcircle of $ABC$. Let $Z$ be the intersection point of the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ with the external bisector of angle $\angle BAC$. Prove that the midpoint of the segment $AB$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ADZ$.
answer: Proof: reflect in the perpendicular bisector $m$ of $AD$ (it passes through the circumcentre $O$): it swaps $A,D$ and swaps the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $AC$, so $Z'=$ image of $Z$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ and $AZZ'D$ is a rectangle; then $\angle AMZ'=90^\circ$ puts $M$ on its circumcircle.

solutions.title: Reflect in the perpendicular bisector of $AD$
solutions.body:
Let $O$ be the circumcentre, $M$ the midpoint of $AB$, $b$ and $c$ the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $AC$ (both pass through $O$, and $Z\in c$). Let $m$ be the perpendicular bisector of the chord $AD$; it passes through $O$, and let $\sigma$ be the reflection in $m$. Then $\sigma(A)=D$, $\sigma(D)=A$, and $\sigma(O)=O$.

**$\sigma$ swaps $b$ and $c$.** The lines $AB$ and $AC$ are symmetric in the bisector $AD$. Since $m\perp AD$, reflecting in $m$ differs from reflecting in $AD$ by a half-turn, which maps every line to a parallel line. So $\sigma(AB)$ is parallel to $AC$. Hence $\sigma(b)$ is the line through $\sigma(O)=O$ perpendicular to $\sigma(AB)$, i.e. the line through $O$ perpendicular to $AC$, which is $c$. Thus $Z'=\sigma(Z)$ lies on $b$.

**$AZZ'D$ is a rectangle.** The internal and external bisectors are perpendicular, so $AZ\perp AD$. Applying $\sigma$, $DZ'\perp DA$ and $DZ'=AZ$. Also $\sigma$ maps each side of line $AD$ to itself (because $AD\perp m$), so $Z$ and $Z'$ are on the same side of $AD$. So $AZ$ and $DZ'$ are equal, parallel and on the same side of $AD$, with a right angle at $A$: $AZZ'D$ is a rectangle. Its circumcircle, the circle with diameter $AZ'$, passes through $A$, $D$, $Z$; so it is the circumcircle of $ADZ$.

**$M$ is on it.** $Z'$ lies on $b$, the perpendicular to $AB$ at $M$. If $Z'=M$ we are done. Otherwise $\angle AMZ'=90^\circ$, so $M$ lies on the circle with diameter $AZ'$. ∎

prompt:
Let $A(n)$ denote the number of sequences $a_1\ge a_2\ge\dots\ge a_k$ of positive integers for which $a_1+\dots+a_k=n$ and each $a_i+1$ is a power of two ($i=1,2,\dots,k$). Let $B(n)$ denote the number of sequences $b_1\ge b_2\ge\dots\ge b_m$ of positive integers for which $b_1+\dots+b_m=n$ and each inequality $b_j\ge 2b_{j+1}$ holds ($j=1,2,\dots,m-1$).

Prove that $A(n)=B(n)$ for every positive integer $n$.
answer: Proof: both are counted by the tuples $(d_1,d_2,\dots)$ of non-negative integers, not all zero, with $\sum_i d_i(2^i-1)=n$ — for type $A$, $d_i$ is the number of parts equal to $2^i-1$; for type $B$, $d_j=b_j-2b_{j+1}$ (with $b_{m+1}=0$).

solutions.title: Encode both by multiplicities
solutions.body:
Let $\mathcal D(n)$ be the set of sequences $(d_1,d_2,\dots)$ of non-negative integers, only finitely many non-zero and not all zero, with
$$\sum_{i\ge1}d_i\,(2^i-1)=n .$$

**Type $A$.** A sequence $a_1\ge\dots\ge a_k$ with every $a_i+1$ a power of two is a multiset of numbers of the form $2^i-1$ ($i\ge1$, since $a_i\ge1$). It is determined by the multiplicities $d_i$ of $2^i-1$, and every element of $\mathcal D(n)$ arises. So $A(n)=|\mathcal D(n)|$.

**Type $B$.** Given $b_1\ge\dots\ge b_m$ with $b_j\ge2b_{j+1}$, set $b_{m+1}=0$ and $d_j=b_j-2b_{j+1}$ for $1\le j\le m$, $d_j=0$ for $j>m$. Then $d_j\ge0$, $d_m=b_m\ge1$, and by downward induction
$$b_j=\sum_{i\ge j}2^{\,i-j}d_i .$$
Hence
$$\sum_{j=1}^m b_j=\sum_{i}d_i\sum_{j=1}^{i}2^{i-j}=\sum_i d_i(2^i-1)=n,$$
so $(d_i)\in\mathcal D(n)$. Conversely, for $(d_i)\in\mathcal D(n)$ let $m$ be the largest index with $d_m>0$ and define $b_j=\sum_{i\ge j}2^{i-j}d_i$ for $1\le j\le m$. Then $b_m=d_m\ge1$, $b_j-2b_{j+1}=d_j\ge0$ (so $b_j\ge2b_{j+1}\ge b_{j+1}$ and all $b_j\ge1$), and the same computation shows $\sum b_j=n$. The two constructions are inverse to each other, so $B(n)=|\mathcal D(n)|$.

Therefore $A(n)=B(n)$. ∎

prompt: Call a rational number $r$ *powerful* if $r$ can be expressed in the form $\dfrac{p^k}{q}$ for some relatively prime positive integers $p$, $q$ and some integer $k>1$. Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive rational numbers such that $abc=1$. Suppose there exist positive integers $x$, $y$, $z$ such that $a^x+b^y+c^z$ is an integer. Prove that $a$, $b$, $c$ are all powerful.
answer: Proof: write $a=\frac{a_1}{b_1}$, $b=\frac{a_2}{b_2}$, $c=\frac{b_1b_2}{a_1a_2}$ and clear denominators; comparing $p$-adic valuations for each prime $p\mid a_1$ gives $v_p(a_1)\,z=v_p(b_2)(y+z)$, so every exponent of $a_1$ is divisible by $k=\frac{y+z}{\gcd(z,y+z)}>1$.

solutions.title: Clear denominators and compare valuations
solutions.body:
By symmetry (the hypotheses are symmetric under permuting $(a,x),(b,y),(c,z)$) it suffices to prove that $a$ is powerful.

Write $a=\frac{a_1}{b_1}$, $b=\frac{a_2}{b_2}$ in lowest terms; then $c=\frac{b_1b_2}{a_1a_2}$. Over the common denominator $a_1^za_2^zb_1^xb_2^y$,
$$a^x+b^y+c^z=\frac{a_1^{x+z}a_2^{z}b_2^{y}+a_1^{z}a_2^{y+z}b_1^{x}+b_1^{x+z}b_2^{y+z}}{a_1^{z}a_2^{z}b_1^{x}b_2^{y}} .$$
Call the three terms of the numerator $T_1,T_2,T_3$. Since the fraction is an integer, the denominator divides $T_1+T_2+T_3$.

**Step 1.** $a_1^z$ divides the denominator, $T_1$ and $T_2$, hence $T_3=b_1^{x+z}b_2^{y+z}$; as $\gcd(a_1,b_1)=1$, $a_1^z\mid b_2^{y+z}$.

**Step 2.** Let $p$ be a prime dividing $a_1$, with $v_p(a_1)=n\ge1$ and $v_p(b_2)=m$. By Step 1, $nz\le m(y+z)$; in particular $m\ge1$, so $p\nmid a_2$ (as $\gcd(a_2,b_2)=1$) and $p\nmid b_1$. Thus
$$v_p(\text{denominator})=nz+my,\quad v_p(T_1)=n(x+z)+my,\quad v_p(T_2)=nz,\quad v_p(T_3)=m(y+z).$$
Since $v_p(T_1)>nz+my$, the power $p^{nz+my}$ divides $T_1$, hence it divides $T_2+T_3$. If $nz<m(y+z)$, then $v_p(T_2+T_3)=nz<nz+my$, a contradiction. Therefore $nz=m(y+z)$.

**Step 3.** Let $g=\gcd(z,y+z)$ and $k=\frac{y+z}{g}$; then $k>1$ because $y+z>z\ge g$. From $n\frac zg=m\frac{y+z}g$ and $\gcd\!\big(\frac zg,\frac{y+z}g\big)=1$ we get $k\mid n$. So every prime exponent of $a_1$ is divisible by the same $k$, i.e. $a_1=p_0^{\,k}$ for a positive integer $p_0$ (also when $a_1=1$). Since $\gcd(p_0,b_1)=1$, $a=\frac{p_0^{\,k}}{b_1}$ is powerful. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. A pair of $n$-tuples $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ and $(b_1,\dots,b_n)$ with integer entries is called an *exquisite pair* if
$$|a_1b_1+\cdots+a_nb_n|\le 1.$$
Determine the maximum number of distinct $n$-tuples with integer entries such that any two of them form an exquisite pair.
answer: $n^2+n+1$: e.g. $0$, $\pm e_i$, $e_i\pm e_j$ ($i<j$); for the bound, group the non-zero tuples by the position $i$ of their last non-zero entry and show at most $2i$ in each group, using that at most $2d$ non-zero vectors in $\mathbb R^d$ can have pairwise non-positive inner products.

solutions.title: Construction and a geometric lemma
solutions.body:
Write $a\cdot b=a_1b_1+\dots+a_nb_n$ and let $e_i$ be the $i$-th unit vector.

**Construction.** Take $0$, the $2n$ vectors $\pm e_i$, and the $2\binom n2$ vectors $e_i+e_j$, $e_i-e_j$ ($i<j$): in total $1+2n+n(n-1)=n^2+n+1$ tuples. All entries are $0,\pm1$ and each has at most two non-zero entries. Two of them have $|a\cdot b|\le1$ unless their supports share two positions $i<j$; then they are $e_i+e_j$ and $e_i-e_j$, with $a\cdot b=1-1=0$. So every pair is exquisite.

**Lemma.** If $v_1,\dots,v_N$ are non-zero vectors in $\mathbb R^d$ with $v_r\cdot v_s\le0$ for all $r\ne s$, then $N\le2d$.

*Proof by induction on $d$.* For $d=1$: non-zero reals with pairwise non-positive products — at most one positive and one negative, so $N\le2$. For $d\ge2$, let $v=v_N$ and project the others onto the hyperplane $v^\perp$: $w'=w-\frac{w\cdot v}{|v|^2}v$. For $r\ne s$ (both $<N$),
$$v_r'\cdot v_s'=v_r\cdot v_s-\frac{(v_r\cdot v)(v_s\cdot v)}{|v|^2}\le v_r\cdot v_s\le0,$$
because $v_r\cdot v\le0$ and $v_s\cdot v\le0$. A projection is zero only if $v_r=\lambda v$, and then $v_r\cdot v\le0$ forces $\lambda<0$; two such vectors would have positive inner product, so at most one projection is zero. The remaining at least $N-2$ non-zero projections lie in the $(d-1)$-dimensional space $v^\perp$ and still have pairwise non-positive inner products, so $N-2\le2(d-1)$, i.e. $N\le2d$. $\square$

**Upper bound.** Let $\mathcal A$ be a set of distinct integer tuples, pairwise exquisite. Apart from possibly $0$, split $\mathcal A$ into classes $\mathcal A_1,\dots,\mathcal A_n$, where $\mathcal A_i$ contains the tuples whose last non-zero entry is in position $i$. We show $|\mathcal A_i|\le2i$; then $|\mathcal A|\le1+(2+4+\dots+2n)=n^2+n+1$.

*Tuples with only the $i$-th entry non-zero:* if two of them had $i$-th entries of the same sign, being distinct integers their product would be at least $1\cdot2=2$. So there are at most two such tuples.

*The others:* for each remaining $a\in\mathcal A_i$, let $a^+$ be $a$ or $-a$, chosen so that the $i$-th entry is positive, and let $\bar a\in\mathbb Z^{i-1}$ be the first $i-1$ entries of $a^+$; $\bar a\ne0$ because $a$ has another non-zero entry. Suppose there were at least $2(i-1)+1$ such tuples. By the lemma (applied in $\mathbb R^{i-1}$; if $i=1$ there are no such tuples at all), two of them, $a\ne b$, have $\bar a\cdot\bar b>0$, hence $\bar a\cdot\bar b\ge1$. Their $i$-th entries are positive integers and all later entries are $0$, so
$$|a\cdot b|=|a^+\cdot b^+|=\bar a\cdot\bar b+a^+_ib^+_i\ge1+1=2,$$
a contradiction. So there are at most $2(i-1)$ of them, and $|\mathcal A_i|\le2+2(i-1)=2i$.

**Answer: $n^2+n+1$.** ∎
